citation: Saif Mahmud, Fadul Sikder, Yuede Ji, Haotian Zhang, Yu Lei. 'The Illusion of Safety: Multi-Tier Verification of AI vs. Human C++ Code'. arXiv:2607.00107v3 [cs.SE], 2 Aug 2026 (v1 submitted 30 Jun 2026). University of Texas at Arlington and NJIT. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.00107
source_tier: Preprint (arXiv, cs.SE); not shown as peer-reviewed.
access_status: Fully read (PDF v3 text extracted and read through the Threats to Validity, Related Work and Conclusion; reference list and tail only skimmed).
sponsor_and_incentive: No funding statement found in the text read. Academic authors; no vendor sells a related product. AI disclosure: GitHub Copilot used for pipeline code, Claude used to help draft and edit manuscript text. Replication package is hosted anonymously.
exact_quotes: Abstract: "AI-generated code is roughly twice as likely as human code to trigger a confirmed runtime violation, even after controlling for code length and test pass-rate." | Abstract: "Under static analysis the two look equally safe, but this is misleading: the apparent similarity reflects code length rather than real safety" | Intro: "of the 661 violations formally proven by ESBMC, 598 occur on untested paths that sanitizers never detect, while sanitizers discover 576 runtime bugs the model checker does not flag." | Sec V-A4: "Programs that pass all functional tests still contain vulnerabilities." | Sec VII: "Programs are drawn from competitive programming tasks and reflect short, algorithmic code. Vulnerability patterns may not generalize to production codebases." | Sec VII: "We use a single zero-shot prompt at temperature = 1.0."
date_and_recency: Posted June to August 2026 (v3 dated 2 Aug 2026). Human solutions are pre-2021 CodeContests submissions; LLM generation done in 2026 with Gemma 3 27B IT, LLaMA 3.3 70B Instruct, Qwen 2.5 Coder 32B Instruct (open-weight models, not frontier agents). Tools: cppcheck 2.19.0, clang-tidy v21, ESBMC v8.0.0, g++ 13.3.0.
key_claims: AI-generated C++ triggers confirmed runtime memory-safety violations (ASan/UBSan) more often than human C++ on the same tasks. Static analysis (cppcheck, clang-tidy) does not separate the two groups and, once length is controlled, reverses direction. Dynamic analysis and bounded model checking flag largely different programs (Jaccard about 0.05), so no single tier is sufficient. Passing the test suite does not imply absence of violations. The gap is stable across three independent generations per model. Authors recommend combining functional tests, static analysis, sanitizers in CI, and selective bounded model checking for safety-critical code.
headline_figures: Sanitizer trigger rate: AI 9.3% vs human 2.6% of compiled programs (3.6x raw; z=9.28, p<0.001). Per model: Gemma 8.6% (173/2018), LLaMA 9.6% (217/2272), Qwen 9.8% (224/2290), human 2.6% (43/1665). Restricted to programs with at least one executed test: 15.5% AI vs 4.3% human. Mixed-effects logistic regression with problem random intercept: adjusted OR 2.15 (95% CI 1.52-3.03, p<0.001, n=4,961). Static (cppcheck, adjusted for LOC): OR 0.68 (0.57-0.81). ESBMC unadjusted OR 1.83 (0.94-3.56, p=0.076), not significant; conclusive human n=96, 13 FAILED. Cppcheck CWE flags: Gemma 45.6%, LLaMA 33.7%, Qwen 36.5%, human 45.1%. Clang-tidy: 27.7%, 33.6%, 29.7% vs human 59.2%. ESBMC FAILED among analyzable: Gemma 25.9%, LLaMA 36.7%, Qwen 29.5%, human 18.8%. ESBMC verdicts over 8,918 programs: 56.5% parse error, 18.2% timeout, 17.4% success, 7.4% (661) failed. 598 of 661 ESBMC violations not triggered by sanitizers; 576 of 639 sanitizer-triggered programs not flagged by ESBMC; 83 sanitizer violations in programs where ESBMC returned SUCCESS; 63 programs flagged by both. Among programs passing all tests: 1.8% of AI vs 3.6% of human trigger sanitizers. Within-model sanitizer variance across generations <=1.8 pp. Pass rate protective OR about 0.23; LOC OR about 6.7 for static flags. Compilation: AI 90-92%, human 98.2%.
sample_unit_and_population: 8,918 C++ programs (7,223 AI: three generations from each of 3 LLMs per task; 1,695 human, up to two accepted solutions per task) across 851 CodeContests competitive-programming tasks. 560 tasks have public tests, 291 have none, so dynamic/cross-tool analysis covers 4,295 programs from test-available tasks. About 12% of Gemma outputs excluded as malformed. Program is the unit, not PR or incident. Zero-shot, no security prompt, OpenRouter default decoding (temp 1.0).
observed_vs_stated: Observed: tool outputs on generated and historical human code. No self-reported belief or human study.
what_makes_trust_justified: Layered verification that executes or exhaustively explores code: ASan/UBSan in CI, plus bounded model checking on safety-critical code, in addition to tests and static analysis. Authors say passing tests is 'necessary but insufficient' and that static-only gates give a false sense of security.
what_it_costs: Sanitizers need test inputs and instrumented builds. ESBMC took up to 60 s per file, timed out on 18.2% and could not parse 56.5% of programs; doubling unwind and timeout (20, 120 s) found 832 failures at 16.8% coverage. Static tools add triage overhead of high-volume style warnings. No human review time measured.
failure_mode_class: Wrong code / security: memory-safety and undefined behaviour (signed integer overflow CWE-190 dominant, heap and stack buffer overflow CWE-122/121, null dereference CWE-476, out-of-bounds CWE-119). Also false assurance from static-only gates.
control_that_would_have_prevented: Not an incident study. Sanitizer-backed CI would have caught the runtime violations on executed paths; bounded model checking caught edge cases on untested paths (e.g. n=INT_MIN overflow that no test and no static tool flagged). Signed overflow was caught by UBSan but not by ESBMC's overflow-check.
limitations_stated: Competitive-programming tasks, short algorithmic code: 'may not generalize to production codebases.' Single zero-shot prompt at temperature 1.0. ESBMC parse error rate 56.5%, unwind 10, 60 s timeout, so FAILED counts are a lower bound; human conclusive ESBMC sample only 96, so formal tier reported descriptively. Sanitizer results depend on test strength and were not stratified by test count. Tool-version bias; clang-tidy run without compile_commands.json. Three open-weight models only. No longitudinal survival in real repos.
counter_evidence: Human code gets more clang-tidy diagnostics (59.2% vs 27.7-33.6%) and among test-passing programs humans trigger sanitizers more often (3.6% vs 1.8% AI), which cuts against a simple 'AI is worse' reading. Formal-tier gap is not statistically significant (p=0.076). Related work cited: Asare et al. found Copilot's vulnerability rates broadly comparable to human programmers'. Human baseline is pre-2021 contest code with likely different selection (accepted solutions only, up to two per task; AI 9 per task). Human solutions compile more often (98.2% vs 90-92%), and Gemma outputs were filtered.

usable_claim: In a 2026 preprint benchmarking 8,918 C++ programs from three open-weight LLMs and pre-GPT human solutions on 851 contest tasks, AI code triggered sanitizer violations at 9.3% vs 2.6% for human code (adjusted odds ratio about 2.15), while cppcheck and clang-tidy warning rates did not show a gap, and tools like sanitizers and a bounded model checker flagged largely different programs. The authors conclude that no single verification tier is sufficient and passing tests is not enough.
do_not_use: Do not generalise to production code, frontier coding agents, or other languages. Do not say AI code is '3.6x less secure' without the contest-code, open-weight, zero-shot context. Do not cite the ESBMC gap (25.9-36.7% vs 18.8%) as significant; the adjusted test was not. Do not say AI code that passes tests is more vulnerable (the opposite held: 1.8% vs 3.6%). Do not state the abstract's earlier 'several times' wording as the adjusted effect; use OR 2.15.
overlap_with_existing_essays: Not checked against the Verification Gap or Checking Isn't Catching essays in this task; the 'no single tier suffices' and 'passing tests is insufficient' points are likely adjacent to their themes [uncertain].
